title: Invasive Moulds: Galactomannan, β-D-Glucan and the Mucorales Ribbon
summary: Use galactomannan and β-D-glucan within their limits, tell Mucorales from septate moulds in tissue, handle tissue so Mucorales survive culture, and know the piperacillin-tazobactam and A. terreus traps.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 60 Hits 9–12 and 16 and Traps 3–6. Checked against Cornely 2019 (global mucormycosis guideline), Donnelly 2020 (EORTC/MSGERC definitions), Fang 2023, Vergidis 2014 (abstract only) and Zoran 2018. Hit 9 and Trap 4 present piperacillin-tazobactam as a current cause of false-positive galactomannan; Vergidis 2014 found none in current US lots (register flag rv-gm-piptazo). Hit 12 calls diabetic ketoacidosis the most common underlying condition; Cornely 2019 describes malignancy as an increasingly important risk alongside diabetes (not flagged; taught as host clue only). Not taught: Aspergillus 3–6 µm width, “lid lifter” colonies in 48–72 h, avoiding cycloheximide media, calcofluor binding chitin and cellulose, BDG high NPV for Pneumocystis.

objectives: State what galactomannan and β-D-glucan detect, their EORTC/MSGERC 2020 thresholds and the fungi BDG misses.
Distinguish Mucorales from septate moulds in tissue and relate host factors to the site of mucormycosis.
Handle tissue for suspected mucormycosis and use direct fluorescent microscopy and culture appropriately.
Interpret galactomannan in patients on piperacillin-tazobactam and recognise A. terreus amphotericin B resistance.

scenes.title: Two molds, two blood tests
scenes.altText: Two patient cards. Patient A: acute leukemia, neutropenic, fever on piperacillin-tazobactam, lung nodules on CT; serum galactomannan index 1.4, β-D-glucan 260 pg/mL. Patient B: diabetic ketoacidosis, black eschar on the palate; galactomannan negative, β-D-glucan negative. A question token: “Two molds — which test sees which?” The cartoon scientist looks from one card to the other.

cues.text: Patient A has leukemia and no neutrophils. She has fever on piperacillin-tazobactam and new lung nodules. Galactomannan and beta-D-glucan are both positive.
Patient B is in diabetic ketoacidosis with a black eschar on the palate. Both blood markers are negative.
Is patient B mold-free? Or is it a mold the markers cannot see? And can patient A’s antibiotic fake a result?

props.label: Two molds — which test sees which?

scenes.title: Two cell-wall markers, two different reaches
scenes.altText: A fungal cell wall drawn as layers (schematic). A galactomannan tag sits on an Aspergillus hypha: EIA reported as an index; EORTC/MSGERC 2020 mycological evidence = serum or plasma ≥ 1.0, BAL ≥ 1.0, or serum ≥ 0.7 plus BAL ≥ 0.8. A β-D-glucan tag sits on many fungi: Candida, Aspergillus, Pneumocystis, Fusarium; its blind spots are greyed out: Cryptococcus, Mucorales, yeast phase of Blastomyces. Criteria card: BDG ≥ 80 pg/mL in ≥ 2 consecutive sera counts for invasive candidiasis and Pneumocystis — once other causes are excluded.

cues.text: Two blood tests look for pieces of the fungal cell wall. Galactomannan is an Aspergillus polysaccharide, measured by enzyme immunoassay and reported as an index.
The 2020 EORTC and MSGERC definitions count a serum or plasma index of 1.0 or more, a lavage index of 1.0 or more, or serum 0.7 together with lavage 0.8.
Beta-D-glucan is broader. Candida, Aspergillus, Pneumocystis and Fusarium all shed it.
But it has blind spots: Cryptococcus, the Mucorales, and the yeast phase of Blastomyces.
In the same definitions, glucan of 80 picograms per millilitre or more in two consecutive sera supports candidiasis or Pneumocystis, once other causes are excluded.

props.label: BDG ≥ 80 pg/mL in ≥ 2 consecutive sera → candidiasis or Pneumocystis (others excluded)

scenes.title: Ribbons versus narrow septate hyphae
scenes.altText: Two hyphae drawn side by side (schematic). Septate mould (e.g., Aspergillus): narrower, regular septa, branching classically ~45°. Mucorales: 6–16 µm (up to 25 µm), non-septate or pauci-septate, ribbon-like, irregular branching; the classic 90° angle is hard to judge in tissue, so width and ribbon shape matter more. Fold artefacts can mimic septa. A risk card: diabetes → rhino-orbital disease; profound neutropenia and GVHD → pulmonary disease. A genus card: Rhizopus, Mucor and Lichtheimia are the most frequently reported agents.

cues.text: In tissue, a septate mould such as Aspergillus forms narrower hyphae with regular cross-walls and, classically, branches at about 45 degrees.
Mucorales hyphae are broad, 6 to 16 micrometres and up to 25, with few or no septa. They look like twisted ribbons with irregular branching.
The textbook 90-degree branching angle is hard to judge in squashed tissue, and folds can mimic septa. Width and ribbon shape are more reliable.
The host is a clue. Diabetic patients typically present with rhino-orbital disease; profound neutropenia and graft-versus-host disease favour pulmonary disease.
The most frequently reported agents are Rhizopus, Mucor and Lichtheimia.

props.label: 90° vs 45° hard to judge in tissue → trust width and ribbons

scenes.title: Handling the specimen and reading the result
scenes.altText: A bench sequence. Step 1: direct microscopy with a fluorescent brightener (calcofluor white or blankophor) — rapid, but does not name the genus. Step 2: tissue for culture is minced or teased, not homogenised (fragile, sparsely septate hyphae); incubate at 30 °C and 37 °C; culture gives genus, species and susceptibility. A caution card on galactomannan: piperacillin-tazobactam once caused false positives through contaminated lots; a 2014 US study found no GM in 32 current lots and 1 of 27 patient sera positive — a rare cause now, but still worth checking. A species card: Aspergillus terreus is intrinsically resistant to amphotericin B — species ID changes therapy. Back to the hook: A fits invasive aspergillosis; B fits mucormycosis that both markers miss.

cues.text: Start with direct microscopy using a fluorescent brightener such as calcofluor white. It is fast, but it does not name the genus.
For culture, mince or tease the tissue. Homogenising shreds fragile, sparsely septate Mucorales hyphae. Incubate at 30 and at 37 degrees. Culture gives the species and susceptibility.

Galactomannan and piperacillin-tazobactam: older antibiotic lots were contaminated and caused false positives. A 2014 US study found no galactomannan in 32 current lots, so it is now a rare cause. Still check the drug chart.
Species matters. Aspergillus terreus is intrinsically resistant to amphotericin B, so the identification changes treatment.
Patient A fits invasive aspergillosis. Patient B fits mucormycosis, which both blood markers miss. The tissue and the culture make that diagnosis.

props.label: A: invasive aspergillosis · B: mucormycosis — markers miss it; tissue finds it

scenes.title: Four classic traps
scenes.altText: Four trap cards appear in turn: “Homogenise tissue for every mould culture” (✓ mince or tease when Mucorales are possible); “GM positive on pip-tazo = false positive” (✓ modern lots rarely cause it — interpret with the clinical picture); “Negative BDG excludes invasive fungal disease” (✓ blind to Cryptococcus and Mucorales); “Treat A. terreus with amphotericin B” (✓ intrinsic resistance).

cues.text: Trap one: homogenise tissue for every mould culture. Mince or tease it when Mucorales are possible.
Trap two: a positive galactomannan on piperacillin-tazobactam is automatically false. Modern lots rarely cause it. Interpret it with the clinical picture.
Trap three: a negative beta-D-glucan excludes fungal infection. It misses Cryptococcus and the Mucorales.
Trap four: treat Aspergillus terreus like other aspergilli with amphotericin B. It is intrinsically resistant.

props.title: ✗ “Homogenise tissue for every mould culture.”
lines: ✓ Mince or tease when Mucorales are possible

props.title: ✗ “GM+ on pip-tazo = false positive.”

scenes.title: Glucan’s blind spots: Crypto and Mucor
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “Glucan is broad but blind to Crypto and Mucor; Mucor makes ribbons — mince, don’t blend.” A glucan searchlight sweeps over fungi; Cryptococcus and Mucor stand in its shadow. A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: glucan is broad but blind to Crypto and Mucor. And Mucor makes ribbons: mince, don’t blend.
Where it breaks: yeast-phase Blastomyces is also missed; a negative galactomannan does not exclude non-Aspergillus moulds; and the ribbon look in tissue still needs culture or molecular confirmation.

props.text: Broad but blind · mince, don’t blend

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “GM = Aspergillus (serum ≥ 1.0, BAL ≥ 1.0) · BDG = broad, blind to Cryptococcus and Mucorales”, “Mucorales: broad pauci-septate ribbons — mince, don’t homogenise · A. terreus resists amphotericin B”.

cues.text: Galactomannan points to Aspergillus, beta-D-glucan is broad but blind to Cryptococcus and the Mucorales, and suspected mucormycosis needs minced tissue and culture.

props.label: GM: Aspergillus (serum ≥ 1.0, BAL ≥ 1.0) · BDG: broad, blind to Crypto + Mucorales
Mucorales ribbons: mince, don’t homogenise · A. terreus: amphotericin B-resistant

explanation.what: Plain language: blood tests can find pieces of fungal cell walls, but each test sees only some fungi; tissue and culture fill the gaps. Scientific terms: galactomannan (GM) EIA index, (1→3)-β-D-glucan (BDG), Mucorales (mucormycosis), septate hyaline moulds, fluorescent brighteners (calcofluor white, blankophor), EORTC/MSGERC 2020 consensus definitions.
explanation.why: GM is an Aspergillus cell-wall polysaccharide released during invasive growth. BDG is present in most pathogenic fungi but scarce in Cryptococcus, the Mucorales and yeast-phase Blastomyces. Mucorales hyphae are broad and sparsely septate, so mechanical homogenisation destroys them before culture.
explanation.measure: GM mycological evidence (EORTC/MSGERC 2020): serum/plasma ≥ 1.0, BAL ≥ 1.0, serum ≥ 0.7 plus BAL ≥ 0.8, or CSF ≥ 1.0. BDG ≥ 80 pg/mL in ≥ 2 consecutive sera (others excluded) for invasive candidiasis and Pneumocystis. Mucorales hyphae 6–16 µm (to 25 µm). Culture at 30 °C and 37 °C; do not homogenise tissue.
explanation.differs: Mucorales (broad, ribbon-like, pauci-septate, irregular branching) vs septate moulds such as Aspergillus (narrower, regular septa, ~45° branching). Rhino-orbital disease in diabetes vs pulmonary disease in neutropenia and GVHD. GM-positive and BDG-positive (aspergillosis) vs both negative with tissue hyphae (consider mucormycosis).
explanation.examAngle: Expect: BDG blind spots, GM thresholds and the piperacillin-tazobactam question, ribbon-like hyphae with tissue handling, Rhizopus as a leading agent with diabetic rhino-orbital disease, and A. terreus amphotericin B resistance.

comparisons.title: Galactomannan vs β-D-glucan
comparisons.distinguisher: Breadth: GM targets Aspergillus; BDG is pan-fungal with named blind spots.

comparisons.title: Mucorales vs septate mould in tissue
comparisons.distinguisher: Hyphal width and ribbon shape; branching angle is unreliable in tissue.

mnemonic.text: Glucan is broad but blind to Crypto and Mucor; Mucor makes ribbons — mince, don’t blend.
mnemonic.explanation: BDG detects most fungi but not Cryptococcus or the Mucorales; broad ribbon-like Mucorales hyphae are destroyed by homogenising.
mnemonic.limitation: Yeast-phase Blastomyces is also missed; a negative GM does not exclude non-Aspergillus moulds; ribbons in tissue still need culture or molecular confirmation.

takeaway: Galactomannan points to Aspergillus, beta-D-glucan is broad but blind to Cryptococcus and the Mucorales, and suspected mucormycosis needs minced tissue and culture.

questions.stem: A patient in diabetic ketoacidosis has a necrotic palatal lesion. A frozen section shows broad, ribbon-like hyphae with few septa. How should the tissue be processed for culture?

options.text: Mince or tease the tissue and incubate at 30 °C and 37 °C
options.rationale: Correct. Mucorales hyphae are fragile; the global guideline advises against homogenisation and recommends incubation at both temperatures.

options.text: Homogenise the tissue in a tissue grinder for maximum yield
options.rationale: Incorrect. Homogenising shreds sparsely septate Mucorales hyphae and can give a falsely negative culture.

options.text: Skip culture; serum β-D-glucan will confirm the diagnosis
options.rationale: Incorrect. BDG does not detect the Mucorales, and culture gives the species and susceptibility.

options.text: Freeze the tissue at −70 °C before culture
options.rationale: Incorrect. Freezing is not the recommended handling and can reduce viability.

questions.stem: A patient with HIV and meningitis has a positive CSF cryptococcal antigen, but serum (1→3)-β-D-glucan is negative. What is the best interpretation?

options.text: Expected: β-D-glucan does not detect Cryptococcus
options.rationale: Correct. Cryptococcus, the Mucorales and yeast-phase Blastomyces are BDG blind spots.

options.text: The antigen result is a false positive
options.rationale: Incorrect. A negative BDG says nothing against cryptococcosis.

options.text: Co-infection with Pneumocystis is excluded, so cryptococcosis is unlikely
options.rationale: Incorrect. The BDG result does not bear on the cryptococcal antigen.

options.text: Repeat the BDG on CSF to confirm Cryptococcus
options.rationale: Incorrect. BDG remains a poor marker for Cryptococcus whatever the specimen.

questions.stem: Aspergillus terreus grows from the BAL of a transplant patient. Why does the species identification matter for treatment?

options.text: A. terreus is intrinsically resistant to amphotericin B
options.rationale: Correct. Section Terrei species show intrinsic amphotericin B resistance, so amphotericin B is a poor choice.

options.text: A. terreus is a contaminant that never causes disease
options.rationale: Incorrect. A. terreus causes invasive aspergillosis.

options.text: A. terreus is intrinsically resistant to all azoles
options.rationale: Incorrect. Reduced azole susceptibility is reported in some isolates, but not intrinsic resistance to all azoles.

options.text: It does not matter; all aspergilli respond the same way
options.rationale: Incorrect. Species differ in intrinsic susceptibility.
